$comment: Naming a property is not pinning it. Before this file the canonicalizer was
correct on every axis below, but correct because JavaScript’s default
comparator happens to match RFC 8785 rather than because anything held it
there. Swapping in localeCompare passed the entire suite while changing the
bytes, because no vector contained a non-ASCII key.
Each case pins one axis where a "JCS-compatible" implementation can silently
diverge. `canonicalUtf8Hex` is the actual pin: hex removes any question of
editor encoding, BOM or escaping. `sha256` is the same bytes hashed, which is
An independent implementation canonicalizes `input`, encodes UTF-8, and

cases.axis: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 — sort by UTF-16 code units
cases.why: U+10000 encodes as the surrogate pair D800 DC00. Its FIRST code unit (0xD800) is below 0xFFFD, so it sorts BEFORE U+FFFD even though its code point is far higher. A canonicalizer sorting by code point, or by locale, puts these the other way round and every hash downstream differs.

Composed U+00E9 and decomposed e + U+0301 are the same grapheme and different strings. JCS does not normalize, so both survive as distinct keys. A canonicalizer that NFC-normalizes collapses them into one and silently drops a field.

localeCompare places "ä" next to "a". UTF-16 code units place it after "z" (0x00E4 > 0x007A). This is the single most plausible well-meant edit that breaks interop, and it passes any test suite that only uses ASCII keys.
Non-ASCII is emitted as raw UTF-8, not as a \uXXXX escape. A canonicalizer using an ASCII-safe serializer produces different bytes for identical input.
